All the member countries of the United Nations are members of the General Assembly, and the position and status of all of them, whether rich or poor, big or small, is the same. Every year the General Assembly meets in its session from September to December and discusses important issues like environment and disarmament. Its significance lies exactly in being a platform where the representatives of the member nations come together, discuss issues of global importance and make policy decisions on them. The decisions are taken by majority and are passed in the form of resolutions.

False.

The very first principle of the United Nations is that all member nations will have the same status. There is no discrimination among nations on the basis of geographical size, economic power or military power. The chapter repeats this while describing the General Assembly: all the member countries are its members, and the position and status of every country, whether rich or poor, big or small, is the same. So the status of the member nations is equal, and the statement is wrong. The chapter does mention that the five permanent members of the Security Council hold the veto power, but the principle it lays down for membership of the United Nations is one of equal status for all.

False.

China is one of the five permanent members of the Security Council, along with America, Russia, England and France, and all five have the veto power. For any decision of the Security Council to be taken, the assent of all five permanent members and four non-permanent members is necessary. If even one of the five permanent members uses his veto, that is, gives a negative vote, the decision cannot be taken. Therefore, if China exercises its veto power, the resolution cannot be passed.

India had participated in the different conferences that were held even before the establishment of the United Nations. India brought issues like decolonisation, disarmament and racial segregation on to the United Nations platform, and in 1946 India was the first country to raise the question of racism in the United Nations. India has always led the discussions about the problems of undeveloped and developing countries. India has also always sent her troops to the United Nations peacekeeping forces, and has even sent an all-woman peacekeeping force. All this shows that India makes serious efforts to solve international conflicts by peaceful means and has played a major role in the work of the United Nations.

Veto is the special negative vote held by the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, namely America, Russia, England, France and China. The Security Council has 15 members, five permanent and ten non-permanent, and for any decision to be taken the assent of all five permanent members and four non-permanent members is necessary. If even one of the five permanent members uses his veto, that is, gives a negative vote, the decision cannot be taken. So a single permanent member can stop a decision of the Security Council by using the veto.

UNICEF stands for the United Nations Children's Fund. It is one of the affiliated organisations, or specialised agencies, of the United Nations that help the organisation in its work by working in a specific area. UNICEF works towards making nutritious food and health care available to children. In India, several workshops were organised by it to find out measures to overcome malnutrition among babies and children. India has made considerable progress towards achieving the millennium development goals with the help of UNICEF and UNESCO.

Two world wars were fought at the start of the twentieth century, and life and property were destroyed on a large scale in these wars. This led to the realisation that there has to be a mechanism to establish world peace. The League of Nations, which was set up after the First World War for this purpose, did not succeed at all. After the use of nuclear weapons in the Second World War, the idea took root that such destructive wars should be stopped, and that stopping them is the collective responsibility of all nations. The United Nations was established after the Second World War to instill this understanding among all nations and to ensure peace and security at the international level.

The peacekeeping activity of the United Nations means creating circumstances that are favourable for bringing about permanent peace in strife-torn areas. The peacekeeping forces help such areas to progress towards peace. In conflict-ridden areas they provide security, and at the same time help is extended for establishing peace. The United Nations takes up peacekeeping as one of its tasks for safeguarding and fostering peace in the world. Along with peacekeeping, the United Nations may also take supplementary actions such as prevention of conflict and mediation, actually establishing peace, implementing the measures of protecting peace, and peace-building. India has always sent her troops to the United Nations peacekeeping forces, and has even sent an all-woman peacekeeping force.

The United Nations is the world's largest international organisation, and it has its own definite objectives. Briefly, the United Nations takes up all the necessary measures for establishing international peace. Its objectives are:

1. To establish friendly relations among nations.
2. To enhance international security by solving international disputes.
3. To safeguard and foster human rights and freedom.

Along with these, the United Nations also aims at enhancing economic cooperation at the international level.

| No. | Organ | Number of members | Functions |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | United Nations General Assembly | All the member countries of the United Nations are members of the General Assembly. Their number has gone up to 193. | To elect the non-permanent members of the Security Council; to choose the United Nations Secretary General and the judges of the International Court of Justice in consultation with the Security Council; to pass the annual budget of the United Nations. It meets in session every year from September to December and discusses important issues like environment and disarmament, taking decisions by majority in the form of resolutions. It only passes resolutions and does not make laws. |
| 2. | United Nations Security Council | 15 members. Of them five are permanent members, namely America, Russia, England, France and China, and ten are non-permanent members chosen every two years by the General Assembly. | Its main responsibility is to maintain international peace and security. In a situation of international conflict it may suggest ending or resolving the conflict and making efforts to establish peace, imposing economic sanctions, or taking a decision of military action against the aggressor nation. It also prepares policies for arms control, and plays a joint role along with the General Assembly in the appointments of the judges of the International Court of Justice and of the United Nations Secretary General. |
| 3. | International Court of Justice | 15 judges, chosen by the General Assembly and the Security Council. Every judge has a tenure of nine years. | To settle the disputes between two or more member nations of the United Nations; to interpret international law authentically; to advise the various organs or subsidiary bodies of the United Nations about legal issues. It is the judicial branch of the United Nations and is located at The Hague in the Netherlands. |
| 4. | Economic and Social Council | 54 members, selected by the General Assembly. Each member has a tenure of three years and each year one-third of the members are newly chosen. | To initiate discussions at the global level on issues like poverty, unemployment and economic and social inequality and to suggest policies to tackle these problems; to discuss and take decisions on issues like women's questions, empowerment of women, human rights, fundamental freedoms, global trade and health related issues; to make efforts to establish cultural and educational cooperation at the international level; to coordinate the functioning of the different organisations working in association with the United Nations. Its decisions are taken by majority vote. |

Chronology of the establishment of the United Nations:

**1941** — The Atlantic Treaty was signed on 14th August 1941, during the Second World War, between the Prime Minister of England Sir Winston Churchill and the American President Franklin D Roosevelt. According to this treaty, a decision was taken to set up a permanent mechanism to establish international security after the Second World War was over.

**1944** — Detailed discussions followed on this decision in a conference among the allied powers, and work went on for preparing a draft of the treaty to establish an international organisation.

**1945** — A second conference of the allied powers was held and the draft was completed. At San Francisco in America, the representatives of fifty countries drafted the Charter of the United Nations after discussions. As soon as the war got over, the Charter was signed on 24th October 1945 and the United Nations was established.

The completed tree diagram runs as follows. At the top is the **United Nations**; below it is its **Headquarters**, which are at New York; and from the Headquarters the diagram branches into two boxes, **Major Organs** and **Affiliated Organisations**.

**Major Organs** — the United Nations has six main organs:
1. General Assembly
2. Security Council
3. Economic and Social Council
4. International Court of Justice
5. Trusteeship Council
6. Secretariat

**Affiliated Organisations** — apart from the six major organs there are many affiliated organisations, called specialised agencies, which work in specific areas and help the United Nations in its functions. Some of the important ones are:
1. International Labour Organisation (ILO)
2. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO)
3. World Health Organisation (WHO)
4. World Bank (WB)
5. International Monetary Fund (IMF)
6. United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
7. United Nations Educational Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO)
